name: GAMBIT
expansion: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Model Behavior & Interactions
tagline: Cooperative and adversarial feature games for the ABCD networks, refereed several ways, with a selection arm kept blind to closure

caveat.text: Internal, exploratory studies. Nothing on this page is an ATLAS result; results are given in words, and the numbers stay in the private repo.

intro.problem: A two-network background estimate [@abcdisco2021] needs its input features split between the networks, and that split is usually made by hand even though features interact and the choice directly decides how well the estimate closes.
intro.value: A principled, data-driven partition would make the background estimate more defensible and show which features actually drive closure, extending distance-correlation feature selection [@das2024] from one network to the assignment between two.
intro.approach: GAMBIT mixes two kinds of game. In the cooperative game the features are players, credited against permutation nulls [@shapley1953][@cohen2005]; in the adversarial game [[nn1-nn2|the two networks]] compete for features [@monderer1996][@rosenthal1973]. The referee sits outside the game as separate arms, and one arm chooses on signals that never see [[closure]].
intro.goals: Run the games under several referees (a dependence test, the reported closure, an expected significance that carries closure as its uncertainty [@cowan2011], and a closure-blind arm), rank every finalist against random partitions run to the end, grade on events no search touched, and state plainly what improved closure costs in discrimination.

questions: Which features actually drive background closure, rather than discrimination?
Does a partition chosen without ever seeing closure, or any partition the games pick, beat the hand-built one and random partitions run to the end, on events no search used?
Does the referee change the answer: do games scored on dependence, on closure, on expected significance and on closure-blind signals pick the same partition?

components.name: August baseline
components.subtitle: Three loss rungs, no game
components.summary: Before any game, both networks were trained three ways in the endcap: plain cross-entropy, with [[disco|DisCo]], and with DisCo plus a closure term. These runs set the working configuration the games inherited.

items.label: DisCo
items.detail: Cut the closure error from hundreds of percent to a few percent. This result stands

items.label: Input scaling
items.detail: Rank-based scaling fitted per fold replaced min-max, which had flattened several heavy-tailed inputs to the first network

items.label: Closure term (withdrawn)
items.detail: Its region counts were [[hard-count|hard counts]], so it had no gradient; its weight only changed [[epoch-selection|which epoch was kept]]. Every result that leaned on it was withdrawn in September and the term rebuilt on [[soft-count|soft counts]]

items.label: An early warning
items.detail: The dependence test could not tell the DisCo runs from the closure-term runs while closure itself moved clearly: the first sign that the referee and the reported quantity diverge

components.name: Cooperative game
components.subtitle: Features as players
components.summary: Each feature's worth is its average marginal contribution to the background estimate [@shapley1953], measured against permutation nulls that give every network its own zero point, so selection needs no hand-chosen threshold [@cohen2005]. Exact values on small subsets, sampled values on the full registry [@wang2022].

items.label: Leave-one-out
items.detail: Every feature scored against shuffled copies of real columns, per network

items.label: Knockout
items.detail: Remove features jointly and check both discrimination and closure

items.label: Pruning
items.detail: Correlated feature families reduced to representatives before selection

items.label: Cross-fitting
items.detail: Choose on one half of the seeds and score on the other, so a winner is never graded on the noise that chose it

components.name: Adversarial game
components.subtitle: Networks as players
components.summary: The two networks take turns claiming, releasing or dropping features, and a move stands only if it beats a measured noise floor. Equilibrium is not guaranteed: coalitions can remove pure equilibria [@kuniavsky2011], and slow convergence can look like none [@panageas2023].

items.label: Moves
items.detail: Claim from the other network, claim from the free pool, or drop

items.label: Gate
items.detail: Paired seeds, a measured floor and a null harness decide whether a move counts

items.label: Worst case
items.detail: Weakest signal mass point kept in the payoff, not the loss [@sagawa2019]

components.name: Pipeline
components.subtitle: Cooperative into adversarial
components.summary: The cooperative stage hands a pruned pool to the adversarial stage, and the result is promoted and graded on seeds neither search ever used. Built and run end to end on the barrel; the data gates in front of it and the endcap run are next.

components.name: Referee arms
components.subtitle: Who scores the game
components.summary: The scoring statistic stays outside the game: a player that chose its own yardstick would pick the one that flatters it. Each statistic runs as its own arm, from the same start, seeds and data, and the finalists are compared. Agreement means the partition belongs to the data; disagreement is itself the finding.

items.label: Dependence (run)
items.detail: The first games were refereed by a G-test on the ABCD grid, $G=2\sum_{ij}O_{ij}\ln(O_{ij}/E_{ij})$, chosen on purpose for a result independent of the reported closure. Its null is chi-square by Wilks' theorem [@wilks1938], so the gate's floor is derived, not measured

items.label: Closure (next)
items.detail: Median [[closure|non-closure]] at fixed cuts, the quantity the analysis reports. It has no derived null, so its floor is measured per region, and the other network's discrimination needs a floor of its own

items.label: Expected significance (new)
items.detail: Asimov significance [@cowan2011] with the [[abcd-prediction]] as background and closure folded into its uncertainty, $\sigma_b^2=\sigma_{\text{pred}}^2+(\text{nc}\cdot A_{\text{pred}})^2$, scored at the weakest signal mass point. Discrimination and closure then trade inside one number

items.label: Closure-blind (designed)
items.detail: Chooses on background [[mutual-information|mutual information]] between the two feature blocks and on per-block likelihood ratios, never on closure or on the dependence test; closure is kept for evaluation on held-out events. See the closure-blind sub-page

items.label: Hybrid (designed)
items.detail: Both scores put in standard deviations from independence and mixed on a circle, $U_\theta=\cos\theta\,z_G+\sin\theta\,\widetilde{|\text{pull}|}$; the two pure arms are its end points

components.name: Closure-blind design
components.subtitle: Selection that never sees closure · design draft
components.synopsis: Choose partitions on signals that never see closure; evaluate closure once, on held-out events, against random partitions.
components.summary: Selecting a partition by its closure and then training the networks with losses that push closure makes the result confirm its own choice: the partition's contribution and the loss's cannot be told apart. This design gives selection, training and evaluation different signals. Selection uses background dependence between the feature blocks [@kraskov2004][@covertthomas2006] and per-block likelihood ratios [@neymanpearson1933][@jaynes1957]; closure is measured once, on events selection never touched, and every arm is ranked against random partitions run to the end.

items.label: Roles
items.detail: Selection: dependence between feature blocks on background, signal information per block, feature-study scores. Training: the locked losses. Evaluation: closure, pull, plane health and expected significance, once

items.label: Event split
items.detail: Events, not only seeds, are split by a hash of their identifiers into a selection half and a certification half; a validation region stays untouched

items.label: Closure-blind signals
items.detail: A tail-weighted test of the background [[copula]] of the two blocks' likelihood ratios against independence [@genest2004], a factorisation likelihood ratio, a [[classifier-two-sample-test|classifier two-sample test]] [@lopezpaz2017], and couplings of a joint [[maxent|maximum-entropy]] model

items.label: Random reference
items.detail: Partitions drawn with no feedback and trained to the end: the distribution every arm is ranked against, and an unbiased check of every proxy, flag and feature score

items.label: Alert flags
items.detail: Model-free checks on every candidate before training: selection-driven separation, dependence that pairwise screening misses, estimator reliability, count features, shared missingness, a dependence trend toward the signal region, split hygiene

items.label: Posterior over partitions
items.detail: Optional: Metropolis–Hastings over the game's own moves on the closure-blind target (a Gaussian-copula mutual information, fast enough for a chain [@ince2017]), with parallel tempering [@swendsen1986] and convergence judged across chains [@gelman1992]; a Hamiltonian variant [@neal2011] only through a continuous relaxation. The target is a generalised posterior [@bissiri2016]

items.label: Pre-registration
items.detail: Endpoints, thresholds and budgets fixed before any run [@nosek2018]; every look at the held-out events logged

page.lede: If the partition is chosen by closure and the networks are then trained to close, a good result mostly confirms the choice. The closure-blind design separates the three jobs. Partitions are chosen on signals that never touch closure or the dependence test on network scores; the networks are trained with the locked losses; closure is measured once, on events the search never saw. Random partitions, run to the end with no feedback, are the yardstick for every arm. This page describes the design; nothing in it has run yet.

sections.heading: Why
sections.text: Decorrelating losses push closure directly. A partition picked because it closes, trained with such a loss and graded on closure, cannot show how much of the closure came from the partition and how much the loss forced at a cost in discrimination. Separate seeds are not enough either: they remove seed noise but reuse the events the choice was made on.

sections.heading: The anchor: dependence of the inputs
sections.text: ABCD needs the background to factorise in the two network scores. By the [[data-processing-inequality]], for any networks $f_1,f_2$ and any loss, $I\big(f_1(X_{S_1});f_2(X_{S_2})\mid b\big)\le I\big(X_{S_1};X_{S_2}\mid b\big)$ [@covertthomas2006]. Background [[mutual-information|mutual information]] between the two feature blocks therefore scores the partition itself, with no network involved. Distance correlation carries no such guarantee. The dependence test used by the first referee arm is already a mutual-information statistic, $G=2N\hat I$, computed on network scores rather than on features.

items.label: Per-feature maximum entropy
items.detail: On its own it does nothing for this problem: marginals carry no information about the dependence between features, and closure is entirely about that dependence. It supplies smoothed single-feature densities for signal and background, and the marginal transform for estimating the copula and mutual information [@jaynes1957]

items.label: Joint maximum entropy
items.detail: A pairwise [[maxent|maximum-entropy]] model of the background, $p_b(x)\propto\exp\big(\sum_j\lambda_j\phi_j(x_j)+\sum_{j<k}\lambda_{jk}\phi_{jk}(x_j,x_k)\big)$. Within that family a partition factorises exactly when every coupling that crosses between the blocks vanishes, so selection becomes a minimum cut on the background coupling graph. It sees only pairwise structure: a dependence that needs two features jointly, such as $x_a\oplus x_b$ against a feature in the other block, is invisible to it

items.label: Mutual information over clusters
items.detail: Objective $\max_{S_1,S_2}\, I(X_{S_1};Y)+I(X_{S_2};Y)-\beta\, I(X_{S_1};X_{S_2}\mid b)$. The signal terms inherit the [[htmiss]] selection, since signal and background sit on opposite sides of it; the independence term uses background only and is clean, and it is the term the argument rests on. Blocks are proposed from pairwise estimates and certified jointly with a nearest-neighbour estimator [@kraskov2004] against a [[shuffle-null|shuffle null]]. With few background events in many dimensions that estimator is biased, so the region with more background carries this arm

items.label: A likelihood to test against
items.detail: Two, both model-free. The factorisation test $H_0:\,p_b(x_1,x_2)=p_b(x_1)\,p_b(x_2)$, whose log-likelihood ratio is exactly $2N\hat I(X_{S_1};X_{S_2}\mid b)$, with a Wilks null when binned [@wilks1938] and a permutation null otherwise. And the per-block Neyman–Pearson ratio $t_k=\ln p(x_{S_k}\mid s)/p(x_{S_k}\mid b)$ [@neymanpearson1933], which gives each block's best possible discrimination with no network. Closure measured on the pair $(t_1,t_2)$ shows how much closure the partition gives before any decorrelating loss; because it is closure, it is used for evaluation only

sections.heading: Why a global test can't certify closure
sections.text: At one cut pair, with background pass fractions $p$ and $q$, non-closure is the log odds ratio of a two-by-two table, and to first order $I(U;V)\approx\tfrac12\,\mathrm{nc}^2\,p(1-p)\,q(1-q)$. The signal region is a tail cell, so the product of pass fractions is small and a tiny amount of information becomes a large non-closure. At realistic cut efficiencies, the information that matters for closure at the percent level is far below the noise floor of any global dependence test on these samples. Mutual-information and copula tests can rank partitions; they cannot certify closure. That is also why the dependence referee missed the endcap knockout: its power is spread over the whole plane, while closure lives in one corner. The closure-blind arm therefore weights its copula test toward the upper tail, $T_w=N\iint w(u,v)\,[\hat C(u,v)-uv]^2\,d\hat C$ [@genest2004], and the decisive closure test stays targeted, on held-out events.

items.label: Closure-blind
items.detail: Payoff $Z_A^{\text{stat}}(t_1,t_2)-\beta\,T_w(t_1,t_2\mid b)$, or the Pareto front of the two terms with a pick rule fixed in advance: expected significance with statistical uncertainty only [@cowan2011], against tail-weighted dependence. Needs no network training during search

items.label: Dependence
items.detail: The G-test on network scores, as in the first games

items.label: Closure
items.detail: Median non-closure on network scores at fixed cuts

items.label: Hybrid
items.detail: $z_G=(G-\nu)/\sqrt{2\nu}$ and the median $|\text{pull}|$ mixed on a circle; dependence and closure are its end points

items.label: Random reference
items.detail: Partitions drawn uniformly within block-size strata, with no feedback and no early stopping on any metric, trained to the end. Each search arm is also compared with the best random partition under its own metric, so a search has to beat best-of-random at the same budget

items.label: Posterior (optional)
items.detail: A generalised posterior $\pi(S)\propto\pi_0(S)\,e^{-\eta L(S)}$ over partitions on the closure-blind target [@bissiri2016], sampled by Metropolis–Hastings with the game's own moves [@hastings1970], parallel tempering [@swendsen1986] and multi-chain convergence checks [@gelman1992]. It gives per-feature placement probabilities and a direct answer to the stable-versus-mixed-equilibrium question. The temperature is not set by the data and is fixed in advance; the copula estimate it uses sees only monotone dependence [@ince2017], so every trained draw is re-checked. A Hamiltonian version [@neal2011] needs a continuous relaxation and is used only if the discrete chain mixes badly

items.label: Pool
items.detail: Every clean feature, including those that separate poorly on their own. Out: constants, the selection-variable families, and anything that separates only through the selection. Redundancy blocks keep their least selection-tied representative, so weak-but-clean features are not dropped by the back door

items.label: High scores
items.detail: Tried first when a network spends its discrimination budget

items.label: Low scores
items.detail: A clean feature with little signal information can still carry background structure; it is tried first for moves that lower dependence between the networks

items.label: Split rule
items.detail: The feature study computes its scores on the selection half only; scores built on all events would leak the held-out half into selection

items.label: Loop back
items.detail: Over the random partitions, each feature-study score is checked against the end-to-end outcome; the score that predicts best orders the next round, and scores that predict nothing are demoted in the feature study

items.label: Selection-driven separation
items.detail: A feature that tracks the selection variable inside either sample, mirrors it, loses its separation next to the selection boundary, or has its signal-background shift explained by its slope against the selection variable. Its signal information is marked low-trust

items.label: Hidden block dependence
items.detail: The blocks are dependent on background while no single cross pair is, or a classifier sees dependence the nearest-neighbour estimate misses

items.label: Estimator reliability
items.detail: The estimate moves with the neighbour count, disagrees between the full sample and its halves, has too few events per dimension, or cannot resolve the level that matters for closure

items.label: Count features
items.detail: Ties broken at random push the nearest-neighbour estimate toward independence, the wrong direction for a check, so blocks holding counts rely on the classifier test

items.label: Shared missingness
items.detail: The two blocks go missing on the same background events, or dependence appears only when incomplete events are included

items.label: Toward the signal region
items.detail: Dependence between the blocks grows across the selection variable inside the background, so independence measured there may not carry into the signal region

items.label: Run policy
items.detail: Only flags that make a run invalid stop it. Every other flag is recorded as a covariate and never used to choose; over the random partitions, the flags are tested for whether they actually predict poor closure

items.label: One look
items.detail: The held-out half is evaluated once, and every look at it or at the validation region is logged; changing the selection signal after a look needs a fresh split or a recorded amendment

items.label: Pre-registration
items.detail: Primary endpoint, hypotheses, thresholds, budgets and the posterior's temperature are written down and locked before any run [@nosek2018]

items.label: Cost
items.detail: Estimated at about two days of compute on one machine, half that on two, set mostly by the search budget of the arms that train networks; the closure-blind search and the posterior chain cost minutes. To be replaced by a measured time before locking

open.text: Does a partition chosen without ever seeing closure close as well as one chosen on it?
Which feature-study score, if any, predicts the end-to-end outcome over random partitions?
Is the posterior over partitions sharp (one stable partition) or spread (a mixed equilibrium)?

Dependence between the input blocks bounds the dependence of any networks built on them, but a global test can't resolve the dependence in the signal-region corner: it ranks partitions and does not certify closure.

Background and signal sit on opposite sides of the missing-momentum selection, so any independence measured on background is an extrapolation into the signal region; the validation region is the nearest check.
The per-block likelihood ratios, the tail-weighted copula test and the posterior sampler are not built yet.

components.name: Directions
components.subtitle: What gets tested next
components.summary: The next round changes the data, the referee and the action space, one at a time where it can. Each direction is written up as a plan in the private repo before it runs.

items.label: New data
items.detail: Move to the new signal and background files; every earlier calibration is redone

items.label: Wider action space
items.detail: Admit features that separate signal from background poorly on their own but are clean, with no filter at the door: a filter scored on closure would be closure feedback. Features that separate only through the [[htmiss]] selection stay out

items.label: Feature-score ordering
items.detail: Scores from the feature study order candidate moves and never gate them: high scores first for discrimination, clean low scores first for moves that cut dependence between the networks. Random partitions then test which score actually predicts the end-to-end outcome

items.label: Knockout search
items.detail: Search around the endcap knockout instead of taking one ladder point, and check the high-score tail

items.label: Mixed equilibrium
items.detail: Test whether the barrel cycling hides a mixed equilibrium, with no-regret dynamics on the recorded payoffs [@cesabianchi2006], offline; in the closure-blind design, also as a posterior over partitions sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo [@hastings1970]

items.label: Seed allocation
items.detail: Spend seeds on promising candidates by successive halving [@jamieson2016] rather than uniformly

items.label: Loss rung as a move
items.detail: Let each network choose its own loss rung while the measurement stays fixed; the prediction is a prisoner's dilemma

items.label: Grid resolution
items.detail: Re-score every recorded game with the dependence test at other grid sizes, offline

items.label: Not deep reinforcement learning
items.detail: The moves are few and each is scored exactly; a learner chasing noisy, costly rewards would amplify the winner's curse. Learning enters only offline, through no-regret dynamics and seed allocation

results.title: August: DisCo carries the baseline
results.text: In the endcap, adding DisCo to plain cross-entropy cut the closure error by well over an order of magnitude. The closure-term gains from the same month did not survive: the term had no gradient.

results.title: First selection-free comparison
results.text: On the barrel, the pipeline's partition, graded on seeds no search had seen, roughly halved the closure error and brought over half the plane's cells within counting noise. The second network lost discrimination and the fold-to-fold scores drifted apart: a trade with a confound, not a win.

results.title: Removing inputs closed the endcap
results.text: Stripping the first network to a handful of features, every calorimeter-energy input removed, cut the endcap closure error by more than an order of magnitude and put every cell of the plane within counting noise, at a modest cost in that network's discrimination. It comes from one knockout ladder and still needs a search and a tail check.

results.title: The dependence referee measures dependence
results.text: Across recorded games the G-test followed distance correlation closely and closure only loosely. In the endcap its verdicts mostly agreed with closure; in the [[barrel-endcap|barrel]] they were close to random against it; across the knockout it barely moved. That is the independent result the dependence arm was run to get.

results.title: Picking a winner inflates it
results.text: In the cooperative game, taking the best of many noisy candidates overstated the coalition's value about twofold. Cross-fitting removed the bias, and the honest barrel ranking still cleared its null, as a list of features to drop rather than to keep.

results.title: Discrimination is not closure
results.text: Barrel features that add nothing to discrimination still do work for factorization; removing them degrades the background estimate. A feature is only safe to drop when both axes clear.

results.title: Equilibrium in one region, cycling in the other
results.text: The endcap game settles quickly; the barrel game cycles. Two features that both networks want and neither can keep explain the cycling, and a disjoint partition cannot express a fix.

links.title: Feature pool
links.text: The feature study supplies GAMBIT's pool, its exclusions and a score table computed on the selection half; GAMBIT's random partitions report back which scores predict the end-to-end outcome.

links.title: Loss configuration
links.text: BASELINE's loss sweeps train on the partition GAMBIT proposes, and GAMBIT takes its working loss configuration from BASELINE's locks.

links.title: Architecture search
links.text: The best architecture may depend on the feature set, so TRUSS and GAMBIT results are read together.

links.title: Grading
links.text: Finalist partitions are graded with the plane-health checks as well as closure.

links.title: Dependence and closure
links.text: Why mutual information between the networks is the closure condition but a weak closure measure, and why a global dependence test misses the signal-region corner.

links.title: Joint maximum entropy
links.text: KERF's maximum-entropy machinery fits the background coupling graph that the closure-blind arm partitions.

open.text: Is there a pure equilibrium in the barrel, or only a mixed one?
Do the three referee arms agree on a partition?
Does a partition chosen without ever seeing closure close as well as one chosen on it?
Expected significance needs a signal yield per mass point; until then it ranks partitions but gives no absolute sensitivity.
The endcap working cut is not yet the same here and in BASELINE; it must be before the two are compared.
The feature study's scores must be recomputed on the selection half of the events before the closure-blind design runs.
